theory.intro: When the derivative of the inner function appears as a factor, the integral collapses back to a single trigonometric function. So $\int f'(x)\cos f(x)\,dx = \sin f(x) + C$. Without that factor the method does not apply.
facts: The **inner function** $f(x)$ is the expression sitting inside the trigonometric function.
$\int f'(x)\sin f(x)\,dx = -\cos f(x) + C$, keeping the minus sign from $\int\sin x\,dx$.
A constant multiple of $f'(x)$ is enough: put the matching fraction outside the integral.

For a power of a trigonometric inner function, use the reverse power rule $\int f'(x)[f(x)]^{n}\,dx = \dfrac{[f(x)]^{n+1}}{n+1} + C$, for $n\ne-1$, rather than the three composite-trigonometric formulas above.
$\int\cos^{n}x\sin x\,dx$ fits the reverse chain rule with inner function $\cos x$, since $f'(x) = -\sin x$.
The method fails when $f'(x)$ is missing, so $\int\sin\left(x^{2}\right)dx$ cannot be found this way.
Check every answer by differentiating it with the chain rule.

For a definite integral, first check that the integrand is continuous throughout the interval, then evaluate the primitive at the given limits without changing them. Do not evaluate a primitive across a trigonometric asymptote.
steps: Choose the inner function $f(x)$ and differentiate it to get $f'(x)$.
Check that $f'(x)$ appears as a factor, up to a constant multiple.
Write the fraction needed outside the integral so the factor inside is exactly $f'(x)$.

For composite sine, cosine or secant squared, use its trigonometric primitive, copying $f(x)$ unchanged. For $[f(x)]^n$, use the reverse power rule to obtain $\dfrac{[f(x)]^{n+1}}{n+1}$, where $n\ne-1$. Add $+C$ for an indefinite integral; for a definite integral, check continuity throughout the interval before evaluating at the limits.

workedExamples.solution_text:
The inner function is $f(x)=3x^{2}+2$, with $f'(x)=6x$. Adjust the constant factor.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int 3x\sin(3x^{2}+2)\,dx\\&=\frac12\int 6x\sin(3x^{2}+2)\,dx\\&=-\frac12\cos(3x^{2}+2)+C\end{aligned}$

The inner function is $f(x)=4x^{3}+1$, with $f'(x)=12x^{2}$. Its derivative is already present.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int 12x^{2}\cos(4x^{3}+1)\,dx\\&=\sin(4x^{3}+1)+C\end{aligned}$

The inner function is $f(x)=4x^{3}+3$, with $f'(x)=12x^{2}$. Adjust the constant factor.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int 2x^{2}\sec^{2}(4x^{3}+3)\,dx\\&=\frac16\int 12x^{2}\sec^{2}(4x^{3}+3)\,dx\\&=\frac16\tan(4x^{3}+3)+C\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text:
a. Differentiate $\sin^{3}x$, and hence find $\int\sin^{2}x\cos x\,dx$.
b. Differentiate $\tan^{4}x$, and hence find $\int\tan^{3}x\sec^{2}x\,dx$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
a.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{d}{dx}(\sin^{3}x)\\&=3\sin^{2}x\cos x\end{aligned}$
The integrand is one third of this derivative.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\sin^{2}x\cos x\,dx\\&=\frac13\sin^{3}x+C\end{aligned}$
b.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{d}{dx}(\tan^{4}x)\\&=4\tan^{3}x\sec^{2}x\end{aligned}$
The integrand is one quarter of this derivative.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\tan^{3}x\sec^{2}x\,dx\\&=\frac14\tan^{4}x+C\end{aligned}$

The inner function is $f(x)=\cos x$, with $f'(x)=-\sin x$. Adjust the sign, then use the reverse power rule.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\sin x\cos^{5}x\,dx\\&=-\int(-\sin x)(\cos x)^{5}\,dx\\&=-\frac{\cos^{6}x}{6}+C\end{aligned}$

The inner function is $f(x)=2x^{2}$, with $f'(x)=4x$. The integrand is continuous throughout the interval.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi/2}}2x\sin(2x^{2})\,dx\\&=\frac12\int_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi/2}}4x\sin(2x^{2})\,dx\\&=\left[-\frac12\cos(2x^{2})\right]_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi/2}}\\&=-\frac12\cos\pi+\frac12\cos0\\&=1\end{aligned}$

The inner function is $f(x)=\sin x$, with $f'(x)=\cos x$. The integrand is continuous throughout the interval.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos x\sin^{3}x\,dx\\&=\left[\frac{\sin^{4}x}{4}\right]_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\\&=\frac{1^{4}}4-\frac{(-1)^{4}}4\\&=0\end{aligned}$

The inner function is $f(x)=\cos x$, with $f'(x)=-\sin x$. The integrand is continuous throughout the interval.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\cos^{4}x\,dx\\&=-\int_{0}^{\pi}(-\sin x)(\cos x)^{4}\,dx\\&=\left[-\frac{\cos^{5}x}{5}\right]_{0}^{\pi}\\&=-\frac{(-1)^{5}}5+\frac{1^{5}}5\\&=\frac25\end{aligned}$

The inner function is $f(x)=\tan x$, with $f'(x)=\sec^{2}x$. There is no trigonometric asymptote on $[0,\pi/6]$, so the integrand is continuous throughout the interval.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int_{0}^{\pi/6}\sec^{2}x\tan^{2}x\,dx\\&=\left[\frac{\tan^{3}x}{3}\right]_{0}^{\pi/6}\\&=\frac13\left(\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)^{3}-0\\&=\frac{\sqrt3}{27}\end{aligned}$

foundation.solution_text:
$f(x) = x^{2}$, so $f'(x) = 2x$ and the integrand is short by a factor of $2$.
$\int x\sin\left(x^{2}\right)dx$
$= \dfrac{1}{2}\int 2x\sin\left(x^{2}\right)dx$
$= -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos\left(x^{2}\right) + C$

$f(x) = \sin x$, so $f'(x) = \cos x$.
$\int\cos x\left(\sin x\right)^{2}dx$
$= \dfrac{\sin^{3}x}{3} + C$

$f(x) = \cos x$, so $f'(x) = -\sin x$.
$\int\sin x\left(\cos x\right)^{4}dx$
$= -\int -\sin x\left(\cos x\right)^{4}dx$
$= -\dfrac{\cos^{5}x}{5} + C$

development.solution_text:
$f(x) = \cos x$, so $f'(x) = -\sin x$.
$\int\sin x\left(\cos x\right)^{7}dx$
$= -\int -\sin x\left(\cos x\right)^{7}dx$
$= -\dfrac{\cos^{8}x}{8} + C$

$f(x) = \sin x$, so $f'(x) = \cos x$.
$\int 6\cos x\left(\sin x\right)^{5}dx$
$= 6 \times \dfrac{\sin^{6}x}{6} + C$
$= \sin^{6}x + C$

mastery.solution_text:
The inner function is $x^{3}$, so $f'(x) = 3x^{2}$.
$\int x^{2}\sin\left(x^{3}\right)dx$
$= \dfrac{1}{3}\int 3x^{2}\sin\left(x^{3}\right)dx$
$= -\dfrac{1}{3}\cos\left(x^{3}\right) + C$
